# Rule of law and separation of powers (`rule_of_law`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/institutions.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Institutions, law & governance (`institutions`)
- Deps: helped by written_law_code, independent_judiciary_judicial_review
- Core idea: The ruler and his officials are bound by the same known, general laws as everyone else. Officials need lawful authority to collect taxes or detain a person, and people must be able to challenge official action before an impartial tribunal. Dividing power can make those limits effective: an assembly can refuse new taxes and judges secure in office can order a prisoner’s release. The argument that convinces rulers is credit and investment: people lend to, trade in and stay in a state that cannot rob them.
- Pitfalls:
  - Confusing rule of law with rule by law: Chinese Legalists wanted strict, published law applied to all ranks, but as the ruler's tool, with the ruler above it
  - Telling a king he is under the law without any body able to make that stick: Magna Carta worked because the barons had armies and the king needed their money
  - Treating Montesquieu's neat three-way separation as a description of England: real systems are overlapping powers that check each other, not sealed compartments
  - Proposing it as an abstract right at a court: questioning the prince's prerogative is treason; it has to be framed as binding bad officials and securing the prince's credit
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1754 BC – Hammurabi presents the king as guarantor of justice for the weak; the king himself is not bound; greece: 4th c. BC – Aristotle, Politics III: it is better that law should rule than any one citizen; Athens distinguishes laws from decrees and prosecutes unlawful proposals; rome: c. 150 BC – Polybius (Histories VI) explains Rome's stability by a mixed constitution of consuls, senate and people checking each other; under the emperors the princeps is held to be freed from the laws; china: 4th–3rd c. BC – Shang Yang and Han Feizi: uniform published law and fixed punishments regardless of rank, serving the ruler; Confucians preferred rule by virtuous men; india: c. 3rd c. BC onwards – dharma texts hold that the king is subject to dharma and may be resisted if he violates it; no institution enforces this; islamic: 8th–9th c. – sharia is held to be above the ruler and is worked out by independent jurists; judges (qadis) are nevertheless appointed and dismissed by the ruler; europe: 1215 – Magna Carta, cl. 39–40: no free man imprisoned or dispossessed except by lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land; 1689 English Bill of Rights; 1701 judges hold office during good behaviour; 1748 Montesquieu; americas: 1787 – United States Constitution builds separation of powers and checks into a written frame
- Read:
  - Montesquieu, De l'esprit des lois (1748)
  - Tom Bingham, The Rule of Law (2010)
  - Francis Fukuyama, The Origins of Political Order (2011)
